entries.example: A complex number is a point on the Argand diagram: z = 3 + 2i is plotted 3 across the real axis and then 2 up the imaginary axis, and that landing point is the number.
entries.meaning: A number of the form z = x + iy, where x and y are real numbers and i^2 = -1: x is the real part and y is the imaginary part.

entries.example: Modulus is the distance from the origin: the line from the origin to z is the hypotenuse of the right triangle with legs x and y, so |z| = sqrt(x^2 + y^2).
entries.meaning: The distance of the point z from the origin on the Argand diagram: |z| = sqrt(x^2 + y^2) by Pythagoras.

entries.example: Argument is the angle; the conjugate mirrors it: arg(z) is the angle of the arrow from the origin, and the conjugate x - iy is the reflection in the real axis, with arg(conjugate of z) = -arg(z).
entries.meaning: The angle arg(z) that the arrow from the origin to z makes with the positive real axis, measured anticlockwise; it is only defined up to whole turns of 360 degrees.

entries.example: Find the principal argument of z^3 when arg(z) = 100 degrees. By De Moivre, the argument triples: 3 x 100 degrees = 300 degrees. But 300 degrees is outside the principal range -180 to 180 degrees, so wrap it by subtracting one whole turn: 300 - 360 = -60 degrees. Hence the principal value is arg(z^3) = -60 degrees.
entries.meaning: The one value of the argument in the principal range -180 to 180 degrees, written Arg(z): every other value differs from it by a whole number of 360-degree turns.

entries.example: Argument is the angle; the conjugate mirrors it: arg(z) is the angle of the arrow from the origin, and the conjugate x - iy is the reflection in the real axis, with arg(conjugate of z) = -arg(z).
entries.meaning: For z = x + iy, the conjugate is x - iy: the mirror image of z in the real axis, with the same modulus and the negated argument.

entries.example: Plot a complex number on the Argand diagram and state its real and imaginary parts
entries.meaning: The plane used to picture complex numbers: the horizontal axis is the real part and the vertical axis is the imaginary part, so z = x + iy is the point (x, y).
